papers.title: Three novel deep-branching orphan protist lineages from the marine rare biosphere
papers.abstract: Metabarcoding has transformed our view of marine protist communities, yet many sequences in environmental surveys are not assigned confident taxonomic identity. These taxonomically ambiguous sequences may include lineages that are not within any known eukaryotic supergroup, which we refer to here as orphan lineages. These orphan lineages matter beyond taxonomy-based community analyses, because they can help us understand early eukaryotic evolution. Here we used phylogenetic inferences and sequence similarity networks (SSNs) of long-read metabarcoding data of the ribosomal operon (18S-28S rDNA) to identify three novel phylum-level orphan lineages. We designate these lineages Deep Orphan Lineages 1-3 (DEEPOLs) and show that they are exclusively marine and part of the rare biosphere, yet ecologically distinct: DEEPOL1 is a cosmopolitan generalist, DEEPOL2 a conditionally rare lineage capable of local polar blooms, and DEEPOL3 a non-polar lineage with a tendency toward the dark ocean. For DEEPOL2, lineage-specific digital PCR (dPCR) combined with catalyzed reporter deposition fluorescence in situ hybridization (CARD-FISH) provides the first in situ visualization of these cells, revealing small, flagellated, and morphologically inconspicuous protists. Together, our results show that substantial diversity remains hidden among rare lineages, and that long-read sequencing combined with targeted molecular and microscopy approaches offers a first step toward linking orphan sequences to organisms and their evolution and ecological roles.

papers.title: Single-cell genomics reveals genomic and functional differentiation between freshwater and saline Achromatium populations.
papers.abstract: Giant sulfur bacteria of the genus Achromatium reportedly contain extensive genomic diversity within individual cells. Most genomic data (35 assemblies) come from freshwater populations obtained from Lake Stechlin, Germany, alongside four single-cell genomes from a salt marsh and saline mineral springs. Here, we characterize marine Achromatium from mangrove sediments in Guadeloupe and compare them with freshwater and saline references. Microscopy, elemental mapping, and Raman spectroscopy revealed calcium-rich inclusions, and intracellular elemental sulfur as previously described for this genus. Scanning electron microscopy revealed two cell-size morphotypes. We generated eleven single-cell, four mixed-cell, and two metagenomic binned assemblies from Guadeloupe mangrove. Divergent copies of conserved marker genes revealed extensive intracellular genomic diversity in individual cells of both morphotypes. Multigene phylogenies provided separation between freshwater references and most genomes from saline environments, including the Guadeloupe population. Gene presence-absence analyses further revealed differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe and Stechlin cells across five functional annotation categories including PFAM, KEGG Orthologs, and CAZymes. Differences in genes associated with osmotic regulation, ion transport, carbohydrate degradation, and secretion systems suggest variation in functional potential related to environmental adaptation, interactions and resource utilization. No significant differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe morphotypes were found. Together, these marine genomes reveal genomic and functional differentiation from freshwater populations and suggest that intracellular diversity does not erase freshwater/saline population boundaries.

papers.title: Depolymerases unmask a conserved receptor to enable phage control of capsulated Acinetobacter baumannii
papers.abstract: We characterized bacteriophage Abs1 that infects clinical Acinetobacter baumannii isolates via the highly prevalent and conserved outer-membrane protein receptor, OprC. However, phage Abs1 is unable to infect capsulated A. baumannii strains as the capsule prevents phage access to its underlying receptor. To circumvent this, we combined phage Abs1 with recombinant depolymerases targeting the major A. baumannii capsule types. In a murine bacteremia model, this combination significantly reduced bacterial burden caused by diverse, capsulated A. baumannii strains.

papers.title: Choosing between Glycolysis and Cholera: identifying glycolipid- and enzyme-based markers of extracellular vesicles in non-model organisms
papers.abstract: The lack of universal markers for extracellular vesicles (EVs) is delaying progress in the field, especially research using non-model organisms. To develop effective options for the detection of EVs, we explored glycolipid-based and protein-based markers. In this study, we show that cholera toxin subunit B (CTxb), which targets the glycosphingolipid GM1 in vertebrates, also binds to EVs from various non-model organisms enabling detection. However, whilst CTxb selectively detect EVs from cell culture and parasite media, it is unsuitable for complex biofluids, such as serum and plasma due to cross-reactivity with high- and low-density lipoproteins. Additionally, we show that the universally conserved glycolytic enzyme enolase is found in EVs from phylogenetically distant species. Multiple highly conserved regions exist across human and several representative non-model organism orthologues, enabling detection of EVs from non-model organism using antibodies against human enolase. Furthermore, the conserved enzymatic activity of enolase enables detection of EVs using an enzymatic assay. Together CTxb and enolase provide a tandem approach for detection of EVs from non-model organisms by targeting different, conserved components of EVs.

papers.title: Enhancing violacein production in an Antarctic bacterial strain: New opportunities for biomedical use
papers.abstract: Violacein is a valuable bioactive metabolite produced by diverse bacteria, including the Antarctic isolate Janthinobacterium sp. UV13. Despite its broad therapeutic potential, large-scale production in native producers is hindered by low yields and the concurrent synthesis of exopolysaccharides, which increases downstream processing complexity and costs. This study employed a sequential statistical approach to optimize culture parameters, enhancing violacein productivity while minimizing exopolysaccharides production in UV13. The methodology included carbon and nitrogen source screening, a Plackett Burman design and a concentration response optimization, followed by chemical inducers evaluation. Results demonstrated that sucrose was an effective carbon source (violacein yield: 32.75 mg/L). Inorganic nitrogen significantly favored violacein synthesis (yield: 28 mg/L, p < 0.05) over organic alternatives which reduced violacein yields 3.4 to 4.2 fold. A single factor central composite design of ammonium sulfate concentration yielded a formulation producing 75.8 mg/L of violacein with an exopolysaccharide titer of 0.91 mg/L. Furthermore, tryptophan was the better inducer, increasing violacein production 2.2 fold (p < 0.05) while simultaneously decreasing exopolysaccharides formation 4.5 fold. The new formulated medium significantly outperformed previously reported conditions, demonstrating that parameter manipulation unlocks UV13 biosynthetic potential for scalable violacein production.

papers.title: Spatial growth within food-like matrices drives physiological diversification and stress adaptation in Salmonella.
papers.abstract: Foodborne bacteria often grow in structured environments, but the effects of spatial organisation on their physiology and subsequent stress tolerance remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how spatial growth in a food-like hydrogel matrix affected the physiology of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and its ability to cope with environmental stresses. Planktonic and spatialised populations were grown for four days in media without NaCl supplementation or supplemented with 6% NaCl. Transcriptomic, extracellular metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses were combined with targeted spatial gene-expression analyses. The multi-omics analyses showed that spatial organisation had a strong effect on Salmonella physiology and induce more physiological variation than the presence of osmotic stress, under the tested conditions. Spatial growth was associated with significant changes in gene expression, carbon metabolism, and membrane fatty-acid composition. Several functions related to stress response and biofilm-associated behaviour were also affected, with corresponding genes showing significant differential expression. When bacteria were grown in the presence of NaCl, spatialised populations showed less transcriptional and metabolic reorganisation than planktonic populations. In addition, gene-expression analyses showed that microcolonies were physiologically heterogeneous, with differences among cell populations within the same microcolony. Spatial growth also associated with the upregulation of functions related to the general stress response, oxidative stress protection, membrane adaptation and acid stress. These physiological changes provide a plausible mechanistic framework for the enhanced gastrointestinal stress tolerance previously observed in spatially grown populations, particularly under acid challenge. Overall, our results show that spatial organisation is an important environmental factor that reprograms Salmonella physiology and can influence its ability to survive stresses encountered after food ingestion.

papers.title: Endogenous serine proteases in MDCK sublines support trypsin-independent influenza A virus replication
papers.abstract: The haemagglutinin (HA) of influenza A viruses (IAV) must be proteolytically cleaved by trypsin-like proteases to mediate fusion between the viral envelope and endosomal membrane of the host cell, a crucial step in virus entry. Most established cell lines rely on exogenous trypsin for the multicycle replication of influenza A viruses. In this study, we investigated various sublines of Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells and found that MDCK-NBL2, MDCK-I, and MDCK-II support trypsin-independent replication of various influenza A viruses, including human, porcine, and avian strains. The serine protease inhibitors camostat and nafamostat mesylate reduced viral replication in a dose-dependent manner. However, the inhibitory effect diminished with increasing viral dose, most likely due to competition between the HA and the inhibitors for binding on the protease. We detected the endogenous expression of several transmembrane serine proteases in MDCK sublines, including TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4. The characterization of these two canine serine proteases showed that TMPRSS4, but not TMPRSS2, is mainly localizing to the plasma membrane. Furthermore, canine TMPRSS4 was more effective than TMPRSS2 in terms of proteolytic activation of various influenza viruses, although there were strain-dependent differences. These results indicate that certain MDCK sublines express functional HA-activating proteases, providing useful models for the replication of influenza viruses without exogenous trypsin, as well as for the evaluation of antiviral strategies targeting transmembrane serine proteases.

papers.title: Recovery of a distant large DNA virus from the genome sequencing of a fish leech
papers.abstract: The leech gut is known to be a viral reservoir, where viruses can persist long-term and are protected from external influences. Therefore, leeches can serve as vectors for transmission of viral disease to susceptible hosts on which they prey. Nonetheless, viral diversity and virus-leech-host interactions remain largely unknown, with hitherto no research directed at identifying viruses that use leeches as their hosts. In the present study, we report the discovery of a novel large DNA virus (phylum Nucleocytoviricota) recovered from genomic sequencing data of the common fish leech Piscicola geometra (Linnaeus, 1761). Through genomic and phylogenetic analyses, we identify this lineage as highly divergent from currently known viruses, with [~]95% of its predicted protein-coding genes showing no identifiable homology with current databases. Whether the leech is a host of this virus or a vector that transmits it to fish species remains unclear. This work highlights the value of off-target sequence retrieval for discovering novel viral lineages and sets the stage for future studies directed towards the prevalence and biology of leech-associated large DNA viruses.

papers.title: Illumina MiSeq, MiSeq i100, and Element AVITI yield concordant ecological patterns for universal 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing
papers.abstract: Molecular microbiome analyses require high-resolution, comparable measurements, often obtained by sequencing marker genes such as the rRNA gene. Recently, new platforms and chemistries have promised to improve performance at lower cost relative to the commonly used Illumina MiSeq 2x300, but have not yet been systematically compared especially for rRNA gene amplicon studies. Here, we compared MiSeq 2x300, MiSeq 2x500, and AVITI 2x300 by sequencing mock communities and field samples via a 'universal' (16S + 18S) rRNA gene amplicons (V4-V5 region) approach. All platforms recovered similar community patterns (Mantel r > 0.93), with no major differences in recovered lineages. MiSeq 2x500 showed ~4.5-fold higher index hopping (5.9 +/- 3.8% vs. 1.3 +/- 1.5%). For 18S, MiSeq 2x500, despite longer reads overlapping the 18S V4-V5 region, only marginally improved taxonomic classification (+0.7% on average) and ASV resolution (+/-1.3%). Meanwhile, all platforms similarly biased against 18S due to its greater length, which we demonstrate can be offset by a gel-based size selection, with no apparent taxonomic bias. Overall the platforms yield ecologically similar results. We highlight platform-specific advantages to help guide decision-making and challenges that can be addressed through dedicated bioinformatic or wet-lab approaches.

papers.title: A conserved MoxR-vWA chaperone complex drives starvation-induced protein degradation in bacteria
papers.abstract: Bacteria must quickly adapt to changes in their environment, notably including the sudden loss of nutrients. We previously showed that in glucose-starved E. coli, widespread starvation-induced protein degradation (SPD) fuels post-starvation proteome remodeling, degrading a wide swath of the proteome to supply the cell with energy and amino acids for synthesis of stress proteins. Here we demonstrate that SPD is mediated by a highly conserved complex of three proteins: the MoxR-type AAA+ ATPase SpdA, the von Willebrand factor A (vWA) domain protein SpdB, and the zinc metallopeptidase SpdC. Structural modeling and in vitro reconstitutions show that these proteins form a complex with 6:1:1 stoichiometry that resembles the widespread, but still poorly understood, family of MoxR-vWA chaperone complexes in bacteria and eukaryotes. Measurements of protein degradation in glucose-starved E. coli cells show that SpdA, SpdB, and SpdC work together to mediate the degradation of SPD substrates. Instead of directly degrading these substrates, our data suggest that limited structural perturbation and proteolysis "softens" SPD substrates and promotes their degradation by the cellular proteases ClpAP/ClpXP and Lon. Thus, SPD enables extensive proteome remodeling during starvation by expanding the pool of proteins accessible to cellular proteases, rather than by increasing protease abundance. Phylogenetic analysis shows that SpdA, SpdB, and SpdC are highly conserved across bacteria, with notable homologs including the well-characterized Bacillus subtilis sporulation factors PrkA (SpdA), YhbH (SpdB), and SpoVR (SpdC).

papers.title: An iron acquisition system promotes Bifidobacterium longum fitness in competitive early life gut communities
papers.abstract: Iron availability influences the composition of the gut microbiota, yet the mechanisms that enable beneficial bacteria to acquire iron and compete within iron-variable communities remain poorly understood. Here, we identify Fei (Fe import), an iron-responsive acquisition system that promotes the fitness of Bifidobacterium longum subsp. longum, a prevalent member of the early-life gut microbiota. Comparative profiling of 20 bifidobacterial strains revealed substantial inter- and intraspecies variation in growth under iron limitation, with multiple B. longum subsp. longum strains maintaining comparatively robust growth. Transcriptomic analysis identified a four-gene locus, feiMQOX, that was strongly induced during iron depletion and returned towards control expression following iron supplementation. The complete locus was highly conserved within B. longum subsp. longum but unevenly distributed across the wider genus. Disruption of individual Fei components impaired growth and reduced cell-associated iron under iron-restricted conditions, while metal-binding studies of purified FeiX demonstrated a physiological preference for Fe(II). FeiX also provided a pronounced fitness advantage during competition with an infant-derived Enterococcus faecalis isolate, particularly under iron limitation. Finally, analysis of longitudinal metagenomic data from Bangladeshi infants demonstrated that Fei is present within infant gut communities and that its abundance changes following iron supplementation. Together, these findings identify a lineage-associated iron-acquisition system that connects micronutrient availability with bifidobacterial physiology and competitive fitness. More broadly, our findings establish strain-level micronutrient acquisition as a potentially important determinant of beneficial bacterial fitness within the developing gut microbiota.

papers.title: Emergence of a Novel Bacteriophage of Toxigenic Vibrio cholerae in Haiti
papers.abstract: Toxigenic strains of Vibrio cholerae O1 are facultative pathogens that persist in estuaries and cause the secretory diarrheal disease cholera. Virulent bacteriophages (phages) can modulate pathogen density in both humans and aquatic reservoirs, thereby reducing cholera transmission. We report a novel phage, MAA01, isolated from cholera stool and environmental water samples collected in Haiti. The MAA01 genome is double-stranded DNA (31,507 base pairs) and contains 47 genes. Based on transmission electron microscopy morphology and phylogenetic analysis, we classify the novel phage as a member of the Caudoviricetes class. Its genome content is consistent with a temperate lifestyle, yet we observed a virulent phenotype in all strains tested, including toxigenic and non-toxigenic environmental O1 serogroup strains. Sequence analysis of spontaneous escape mutants of V. cholerae identified the O1 lipopolysaccharide antigen as the phage receptor. Using an infant mouse model of intestinal colonization, we showed that MAA01 can reduce V. cholerae load by 4-fold, indicating it can prey on its host in the small intestine.

papers.title: Energetic niches of syntrophic methanogens recorded by clumped isotopes
papers.abstract: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, an important energy source and a potential biosignature in extraterrestrial environments. Stable carbon and hydrogen isotope ({delta}13C and {delta}D) and clumped isotopologues ({triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2) compositions of methane have been widely used as tracers for methanogenesis pathways. Furthermore, isotopic signatures of methane typically shift closer to equilibrium as the Gibbs energy ({triangleup}Gr) of methanogenesis moves closer to the energy limit of life. However, the variations of clumped methane isotope signatures in response to the changes in {triangleup}Gr lack careful examination. In this study, we measure the isotope signatures of methane produced by monoculture methanogens with formate or H2/CO2, and by syntrophic cocultures of hydrogenotrophic methanogens paired with acetate or propionate oxidizers. Methanogenesis by cocultures has lower Gibbs energy yield than monocultures, yet both {triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2 values from cocultures are further away from isotopic equilibrium. From these experiments, we identify an energetic niche ({triangleup}Gr ~ -35 kJ mol-1 CH4), where {delta}13C, {triangleup}13CH3D and {triangleup}12CH2D2 values of hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis transiently exhibit more disequilibrium. This study presents differential responses of bulk carbon, hydrogen and clumped isotopic signatures to {triangleup}Gr, and highlights their applications in distinguishing methanogenesis under different energy regimes.

papers.title: Identification and characterization of a Streptococcus strain isolated from the esophagus of an adult male heterozygous for the CF allele
papers.abstract: The genus Streptococcus consists of diverse bacteria that are integral components of the human microbiome, acting as both important commensals and opportunistic pathogens. In this study, one strain of an -hemolytic species of the genus Streptococcus, GP0011T, isolated from an esophageal aspirate collected during an endoscopy, was characterised phenotypically to establish its taxonomic status. The strain was isolated from an adult male heterozygous for a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) mutation. The phylogenetic analysis indicates that the strain is a novel species within the mitis group, with Streptococcus oralis ATCC 35037T being the closest relative with 94.84% average nucleotide identity (ANI) and 58.3% digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH). Phenotypic characterization and API20 Strep strips distinguished GP0011T from S. oralis by the absence of alkaline phosphatase activity, trehalose fermentation, and starch fermentation, and by superior growth on D-mannitol and D-sorbitol, consistent with genomic data. The strain is Gram-positive, catalase-negative, and the cells are ovoid with a mean cell diameter of 1.3 {micro}m. Growth occurred at 25-43 C, with an optimum at 30 C, with an optimum at pH 8.0. Antibiotic resistance genes msrD and mefA, conferring resistance to azithromycin and erythromycin, as well as pathways for mannitol and sorbitol metabolism, were found and phenotypically confirmed in the GP0011T genome but were absent from S. oralis. These findings indicate that GP0011T represents a novel species within the genus Streptococcus with the proposed name of Streptococcus ruoffae sp. nov. The type strain is GP0011T (ATCC TSD-627 and NCTC 15312).

papers.title: Genomic blueprints of a dynamic deep sea: contrasting adaptive strategies potentially drive seasonal microbial succession
papers.abstract: Genetic variation within marine microbial populations can help reveal how deep-sea communities respond to environmental change. However, population-level genomic variation in deep pelagic waters remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic datasets from ~1,080 m depth in the South China Sea to compare genomic variation between summer and winter microbial assemblages. Among 11 persistent metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) detected in both summer and winter samples, we observed differences in abundance, nucleotide diversity ({pi}), pN/pS ratios, and gene-level differentiation. Two enriched populations showed contrasting patterns, with Sphingobium yanoikuyae enriched in winter samples and Methyloversatilis universalis enriched in summer samples. The winter-enriched S. yanoikuyae population carried winter-associated accessory genes related to restriction-modification and toxin-antitoxin systems, consistent with a defense-oriented persistence profile. In contrast, the summer-enriched M. universalis population showed higher nucleotide diversity in summer samples and divergence in genes related to motility, transport, and cobalamin acquisition. Across persistent MAGs, low pN/pS ratios indicated predominantly purifying selection, whereas gene-specific divergence and flexible accessory gene content suggested population-level adaptive potential under contrasting winter and summer conditions. These results reveal population-genomic differences associated with winter-summer microbial shifts in the deep sea.

papers.title: Formate, hydrogen, and acetate shape the morphology, physiology and lifestyles of the host-associated methanogen Methanobrevibacter smithii
papers.abstract: Methane-producing archaea (methanogens) are increasingly linked to gastrointestinal, neuropsychiatric, and neurodevelopmental disorders. These conditions are often associated with altered microbial metabolism that changes the availability of acetate, formate, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane in the gut. However, the physiological importance of formate and acetate in host-associated methanogens remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to interpret microbiome data and infer functions and cross-domain interactions of methanogens in health and disease. Here, we investigated the physiological and metabolic capabilities of Methanobrevibacter smithii, the predominant methanogen of the human gut. Formate limitation altered growth, morphology, extracellular pH, gas metabolism, and cellular organization, and induced the formation of cell aggregates. Although acetate was consumed only in small quantities (nmol), its availability significantly influenced growth, gas metabolism, extracellular pH, and formate utilization, indicating functions that extend beyond its role as a biosynthetic precursor. Conversely, nutrient excess promoted a transition to a biofilm lifestyle, suggesting that biofilm formation may function as a carbon sink. We further developed Msm_MEP, an experimentally refined genome-scale metabolic model based on the AGORA2 reconstruction, which captures the metabolic capabilities of M. smithii, quantifies ATP allocation across cellular processes, and predicts the phenotypic consequences of gene deletions. Together, our findings identify formate, hydrogen, and acetate as interacting determinants of M. smithii physiology and suggest metabolite-dependent transitions between planktonic growth, cell aggregation, and biofilm formation. Our results establish a framework for interpreting microbiome data and understanding how environmental metabolites shape archaea physiology and cross-domain interactions within the human microbiome.

papers.title: TRIM5α, TRIM56 and TRIM69 differentially regulate dengue virus 2 infection through selective NS2B3-mediated antagonism
papers.abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) is a major mosquito-borne human pathogen. Understanding the mechanisms of cellular resistance to the infection is vital to develop novel therapeutic tools. Tripartite motif (TRIM) proteins contribute to antiviral innate immunity through direct restriction of viral replication and regulation of antiviral signaling, but current knowledge on DENV targeting by TRIM proteins remains preliminary. Previously, TRIM56 was found to inhibit DENV, whereas reports on whether TRIM69 is a DENV restriction factor are conflicting. Surprisingly, the broad-spectrum viral restriction factor TRIM5 was proposed to restrict tick-borne but not mosquito-borne flaviviruses. Here, we investigated the effects of TRIM5, TRIM56, and TRIM69 on DENV serotype 2 (DENV2) infection. Overexpression experiments showed that TRIM5 and TRIM56 restrict DENV2, whereas TRIM69 enhances it. Consistently, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss-of-function showed that knocking out TRIM5 or TRIM56 increases infection, while TRIM69 knockout decreases it. Restriction correlated with reduced viral RNA and viral protein levels in TRIM5- and TRIM56-expressing cells. Virus-free experiments showed that TRIM56 downregulates the DENV2 protease complex NS2B3 levels. Reciprocally, DENV2 NS2B3 reduced TRIM56 and TRIM69 abundance independently of protease activity. RING domain-mutated TRIM56 retained partial antiviral activity and the ability to reduce NS2B3 levels, and TRIM56-NS2B3 reciprocal downmodulation effects were not counteracted by proteasomal or lysosomal inhibition. Together, these findings establish TRIM5 as a DENV2 restriction factor, reveal TRIM69 as a positive factor in DENV2 infection, suggest that TRIM5? and TRIM56 inhibit DENV2 through distinct mechanisms, and hint at proteasome-independent TRIM56-NS2B3 reciprocal downmodulation.

papers.title: Capsular surveillance-guided phage cocktails against carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
papers.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is among the most urgent antimicrobial-resistance threats, yet its extraordinary capsular diversity has kept phage therapy locked in per-isolate matching-a process too slow and labor-intensive for routine use. Here we convert this specificity problem into a look-up problem. Interrogating 26,138 CRKP genomes from 96 countries, we show that capsular diversity collapses onto a tractable target list: 14 capsular locus (KL) types dominate contemporary circulation and jointly account for 67-77% of the CRKP burden in every WHO region, stably from 2010 to 2024 and after removal of sampling bias. We assembled a repository of 48 strictly lytic phages spanning all 14 types and organized it into capsule-defined modules: for eight KL types a single capsule-targeting phage sufficed to prevent resistant regrowth over 24 h, and for the remaining six a two-phage module pairs a capsule-targeting phage with a capsule-independent phage that recognizes the second receptor layer exposed upon capsule loss. We treated 28 clinical isolates, covering two distinct STs for each of the 14 KL types. Modules were assigned from the KL call alone, without isolate-level matching data. Growth was suppressed in every strain, and ST background had no significant effect in 12 of 14 types. These results establish capsule type, not lineage, as the operative unit of CRKP phage preparedness: a single rapid KL-typing step converts a diagnostic result into a therapeutic decision, providing a practical, lineage-agnostic route from surveillance to treatment.

papers.title: Treponema pallidum eight-stranded beta-barrels: an evolving, versatile family of outer membrane proteins in the service of stealth pathogenicity.
papers.abstract: Syphilis is a multistage sexually transmitted infection caused by the highly invasive and immunoevasive spirochete Treponema pallidum (TPA). TPA depends on the import of many host-derived nutrients to sustain its auxotrophic lifestyle. Moreover, its invasive nature requires interactions with diverse host molecules to successfully disseminate and persist. The outer membrane proteins (OMPs) mediating these processes remain largely uncharacterized. In other bacteria, 8-stranded {beta}-barrels (8S{beta}Bs) perform such functions, including nutrient uptake and host interactions. Here, we investigated the composition, structural diversity and evolutionary dynamics of the 8S{beta}B family in TPA. Reexamination of the TPA OMPeome revealed four previously unrecognized members in addition to the four known 8SBs, expanding the family to eight members. Based on RNAseq, all eight were transcribed in treponemes harvested from rabbit testes. Predicted structures revealed substantial differences in channel properties and extracellular loop (ECL) architecture, consistent with functional diversification. AlphaFold 3 modeling predicted interactions with diverse host molecules implicated in nutrient uptake, adherence, and immune regulation, providing testable hypotheses for the functional specialization of individual 8SBBBs. Despite containing predicted B-cell epitopes, most TPA 8S{beta}B ECLs exhibited limited antigenicity during rabbit infection. Analysis of global clinical strains revealed distinct patterns of sequence variation across the 8S{beta}B family, although most were highly conserved and appeared to be under purifying selection. Variation within hypermutable intragenic polyguanosine tracts emerged as an additional potential mechanism for modulating 8S{beta}B repertoire composition. Our findings highlight the 8S{beta}B family as an important component of the molecular architecture underlying TPA stealth pathogenicity and reveal an ongoing mechanism through which the spirochete diversifies its OMP repertoire within circulating populations.

papers.title: Development of an Enclosed Microbial Co-culture Device and GCXGC-TOFMS Workflow to Investigate Volatile Organic Compound Exchange
papers.abstract: Microbial volatile organic compounds (mVOCs) can mediate interactions between microorganisms without direct physical contact. However, co-culture systems to examine these interactions are limited, and volatilomic data interpretation is challenging. Here, we developed enclosed microbial co-culture platforms compatible with diverse microbial systems, headspace solid-phase microextraction (HS-SPME), and comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GCXGC-TOFMS) for mVOC sampling and characterization. In a double-layer co-culture device, diffusion of exogenously supplemented Aspergillus fumigatus mVOCs, 1-octen-3-ol and isopentyl alcohol, inhibited Pseudomonas aeruginosa growth and biofilm formation. The device was then used to examine mVOC-mediated interkingdom interactions between the bacterium P. aeruginosa and the spore-forming fungus A. fumigatus. GCXGC-TOFMS was used to profile mVOCs in four sample classes: media, each individual monoculture, and co-culture. Tile-based F-ratio analysis identified 198 analyte hits that differed across at least two of the four sample classes. Subsequent ANOVA identified 104 of these analytes as statistically significant (p < 0.01). To systematically classify their abundance patterns, pairwise comparisons among the four sample classes were encoded using a six-digit ternary code representing the direction and statistical significance of each difference. Of the 104 significant analytes, 88 were assigned to 15 recurring ternary-code groups, capturing distinct patterns associated with microbial production, suppression in co-culture, and differential consumption of media-derived compounds. Closely related ternary-code groups were further consolidated into five major Categories, providing biologically interpretable mVOC profiles. Overall, the integrated co-culture platform and analytical approach provide a versatile framework for investigating microbial volatile interactions and interpreting complex multidimensional volatilomic datasets.

papers.title: Periodic spatial patterning of gene expression via a natural quorum-synchronized oscillator
papers.abstract: In many biological systems, genetic oscillators that function in growing tissues can establish spatially repetitive patterns of gene expression. However, few mechanisms for generating such patterns are known in bacteria. Here, we describe an oscillator within the quorum sensing circuit of Streptomyces coelicolor. Through modeling and genetic experiments, we demonstrate that this quorum oscillator controls periodic expression of a gene involved in antibiotic biosynthesis at the periphery of expanding colonies. We show that environmental factors, namely small molecule diffusabilty and carrying capacity, independently modulate the oscillator frequency and amplitude, respectively. The architecture of the quorum oscillator imbues this "clock" with three emergent features; it is synchronized locally across cells, only advances due to collective cellular communication, and its dynamics are directly responsive to environmental conditions.

papers.title: Sugar alternatives shift the evolutionary trajectory of fluoride resistance in cariogenic and non-cariogenic dental bacteria
papers.abstract: Dental caries result from acidogenic biofilms dissolving enamel while growing on fermentable dietary sugars. While fluoride from toothpastes and professional products is widely used for caries control, sugar alternatives with inhibitory effects on some dental microbiota (e.g., erythritol and xylitol) instead reduce the cariogenicity of foods and act as prebiotics, often in combination with of fluoride, to control caries progression. Despite their growing prevalence, we do not understand how frequent exposure to sugar alternatives impacts the evolutionary pressures faced by oral bacteria. Herein, we tested the effects of carbon source (glucose, sorbitol, erythritol, or xylitol) on the modes and effectiveness of evolving fluoride resistant cariogenic (S. mutans) and non-cariogenic (S. gordonii) populations. For S. gordonii, evolving in glucose resulted in significantly more non-synonymous mutations compared to populations evolving in sugar alternatives (erythritol, sorbitol, xylitol), but without a drastic increase in fluoride resistance. Contrastingly, for cariogenic S. mutans, evolving in the presence of fermentable sugars resulted in much greater fluoride resistance, but without higher numbers of substitutions relative to those found in isolates from populations evolved in the presence of non-fermentable sugars. We observed previously unreported fluoride resistance mutations across carbon conditions, including a case of parallel evolution in the histone-like binding protein (smu_589) in S. mutans isolates evolved in environments with fluoride and a variety of sugar alternatives. Together, these results demonstrate that commonly used sugar alternatives can shape the evolutionary trajectory of dental microbiota to a broad stressor, such as fluoride.

papers.title: Efficient Method for Estimating the Frequency of Plasmidless Cell Generation per Cell Division
papers.abstract: Plasmids are self-replicating pieces of DNA that play a major role in the evolution and spread of adaptive genes in bacteria. Plasmids tend to form stable associations with their hosts, including plasmids such as small, multicopy plasmids that typically lack specialized partition and horizontal transfer systems. Using a ColE1 plasmid model, we present a method that quantifies the frequency of plasmid loss over a short, defined time window. This method is based on the transient survival of plasmidless cells in the presence of selecting antibiotic and it has two main advantages over plasmid visualization approaches: (1) it does not require modifications in plasmid sequence, preventing artifactual results linked to sequence alteration, and (2) it can unambiguously resolve plasmidless cells relative to cells with a low plasmid copy number. Thus, our approach is ideal for the study of the stability of naturally-occurring small, multicopy plasmids or for the identification of modulators of stability. Using our method, we describe a mutant whose long-term stability is exclusively dependent on increased accurate segregation. Finally, we report that moderate sequence manipulations (outside ori sequence) do not have a major impact on early plasmid loss, which is relevant for the design of plasmid tagging approaches.

papers.title: Unravelling bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis in the uncultured Roseilinea
papers.abstract: Filamentous anoxygenic phototrophs (FAPs) of the Chloroflexota phylum are abundant members of microbial mat communities. All isolated and culturable FAPs are found in a single class within this phylum, but metagenomic studies of hot spring communities from around the world have indicated that phototrophic members of an additional class may exist, which have so far eluded cultivation for study in the laboratory. Metagenome-assemble genomes (MAGs) of these "Candidatus Roseilinea" species all lack genes encoding the central enzymes of bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis common to all FAPs and to the seven other diverse phyla of anoxygenic phototrophs, which could indicate that these organisms are no longer phototrophic or that they employ a novel set of enzymes to generate chlorophyllide from magnesium protoporphyrin IX. Here we demonstrate that the five terminal enzymes of bacteriochlorophyll biosynthesis encoded in the MAG of Japanese hot spring-dwelling "Ca. Roseilinea sp. NK_OTU-006" are active and restore pigment production and phototrophic growth in a set of mutants of the model purple phototrophic bacterium Rhodobacter sphaeroides. While many organisms are known to require exogenous supply of metabolically costly modified tetrapyrroles such as vitamin B12 for growth, the retained function of the tested Roseilinea enzymes and the restriction of these species to dense microbial mats leads us to hypothesise that these organisms may be the first examples of bacteriochlorophyll auxotrophs. We suggest that Roseilinea scavenge pigment precursors and/or breakdown products excreted by other members of the mat to generate the mature bacteriochlorophyll they require to perform phototrophy, an exchange that we demonstrate can occur between Rhodobacter sphaeroides mutants. We further suggest that future attempts to isolate Roseilinea species should employ the exogenous supplementation of (bacterio)chlorophyllide into culture medium.

papers.title: Carbon allocation strategies across Mucoromycota and the discovery of oxalic acid secretion in Absidia
papers.abstract: In this work, nine strains representing eight species, seven genera, and five families from the phylum Mucoromycota were studied for their production of biomolecules (lipids, saccharides, phosphates, organic acids, ethanol, and glycerol) under cultivation in media with different carbon-to-nitrogen (low, medium, and high). Although lipid accumulation was a common feature across the species, the results revealed also differences in carbon allocation strategies between families, both in magnitude and nature of the biomolecules produced. In general, members of Mucoraceae allocated carbon and energy toward the production of lipids, polyphosphates, organic acids, ethanol and glycerol; Mortierellaceae toward lipids, saccharides, and to a lesser extent to organic acids; Cunninghamellaceae toward lipids, phosphates, and saccharides; Lichtheimiaceae toward lipids and saccharides; and Umbelopsidaceae toward lipids, phosphates, and slightly to organic acids. In addition, genus-specific differences were observed within some families, most notably the secretion of organic acids by species of Rhizopus (Mucoraceae) and Absidia (Cunninghamellaceae). Remarkably, Absidia glauca allocated carbon to the production of organic acids independently of the medium C/N ratio. This unusual observation motivated further experiments, which resulted in the identification of oxalic acid in four different strains of A. glauca and other five Absidia species. The secretion of oxalic acid likely occurs across multiple species of Absidia. These findings suggest that oxalic acid secretion may be a broader metabolic trait within the genus Absidia. To our knowledge, this is the first report of oxalic acid secretion in Absidia species, revealing a previously unrecognized metabolic capability within the phylum Mucoromycota.

papers.title: A de novo FtsA binder blocks late divisome recruitment, unmasking a hidden constriction mechanism
papers.abstract: Bacterial cytokinesis requires assembly of a multiprotein divisome complex, but the molecular event triggering its midcell recruitment and activity remains unclear. Recent work suggests a transition in the oligomeric structure of the conserved actin homolog FtsA may activate the divisome complex in Escherichia coli. Here, we test this model using a de novo designed protein binder, L125, predicted to block longitudinal FtsA oligomerization. L125 localizes to the Z-ring and inhibits cell division by blocking recruitment of late divisome proteins while enhancing recruitment of early division proteins. These findings implicate the FtsA longitudinal oligomerization interface in late divisome recruitment. Unexpectedly, L125-treated cells form broad, shallow constrictions that fail to complete division. These constrictions occur despite loss of detectable late-divisome localization and are consistent with ZipA-dependent preseptal cell-wall synthesis, previously not known to cause constrictions. This alternative constriction pathway may reinforce the future division site before activation of the canonical division machinery.

papers.title: Grape branch substrates promote adaptive glycerophospholipid metabolism and lipid-synthesis gene expression in Stropharia rugosoannulata under moderate nitrogen limitation
papers.abstract: This study investigated the use of lignified grape plant materials (branches, stems, and roots) as cultivation substrates for Stropharia rugosoannulata and their effects on fruiting-body lipid metabolism. Metabolomic profiling identified glycerophospholipid metabolism as the primary pathway showing differential responses among substrates. While overall lipid composition remained largely unchanged, intermediate Lyso-GPL metabolites (LPA, LPC, LPI, and LPS) were more active under grape-branch substrates, indicating enhanced membrane-lipid metabolic remodeling. Simulation experiments with varying C/N ratios demonstrated that moderate nitrogen limitation (C/N = 28:1) significantly upregulated key lipid-synthesis genes (ACS1, ACS2, ACC, and FAS), with ACS1 showing the strongest response, and also activated the transcription factor GCN4. Under severe nitrogen limitation (C/N = 64:1), ACS1 upregulation persisted but GCN4 activation did not, suggesting a transition toward metabolic suppression. These findings indicate that moderate nitrogen restriction, characteristic of grape-branch substrates, preferentially engages adaptive lipid-metabolic regulatory networks that may improve mushroom quality.

papers.title: Growth-supporting reductive defluorination by an amino acid-fermenting bacterial isolate
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), also known as "forever chemicals", are ubiquitous environmental pollutants, highly persistent and toxic to humans and ecosystems. In addition to legacy PFAS, largely alkanoic acids, perfluorinated olefins and their corresponding enoic acids are emerging PFAS of concern. However, reported PFAS biodegradation is typically not growth-supporting, hindering the selection for effective defluorinating bacteria. Here, we report a new amino acid-fermenting bacterial isolate, Sedimentibacter sp. strain ZM-1, that performs high-rate reductive defluorination of a perfluoroenoic acid at physiologically relevant levels (mM). This process substantially enhanced energy conservation and cell growth, with three times higher growth than fermenting L-arginine alone and 50% higher than Stickland fermentation. The reductive defluorination redirected excess reducing equivalents (NADH) away from reducing protons and internal fermentation intermediates, as evidenced by decreased H2 production and downregulation of several NADH-dependent electron-bifurcating oxidoreductases. This defluorinating electron shunting drove arginine fermentation and oxidation of intermediates, such as ornithine and alanine, to form more acetate and CO2, leading to higher substrate-level ATP synthesis per arginine consumed. This process also generated reduced ferredoxin available for cell synthesis or anaerobic respiration, as genes involved in these processes were significantly upregulated. ZM-1 has a unique and effective CLCF-type fluoride exporter that works with the highly efficient defluorinating system to enable fluorotrophic growth. Since amino acid-fermenting anaerobes are common in the environment, such fluorotrophy opens new paths for natural selection of defluorination to drive natural and laboratory evolution of fluorophilic bacteria.

papers.title: Capsidiol-inducible MFS gene BcmfsCi contributes to host-dependent virulence in the generalist fungal pathogen Botrytis cinerea
papers.abstract: Broad-host-range plant pathogens must cope with chemical defenses that differ among host plants. This study focused on fungal genes responsive to capsidiol, a sesquiterpenoid phytoalexin produced by plants of the genera Capsicum and Nicotiana. RNA-seq analysis of the gray mold fungus Botrytis cinerea identified Bcin15g00040 as a gene strongly induced by capsidiol but not by rishitin or resveratrol. This gene was designated BcmfsCi and selected for functional characterization. The gene was predicted to encode a major facilitator superfamily (MFS) protein with 12 transmembrane helices. Promoter-GFP reporter analysis showed selective responses to capsidiol and capsidiol 3-acetate among the five terpenoids tested. Promoter activity was also detected in infected tissues of Nicotiana benthamiana and Capsicum annuum (bell pepper). Two independent BcmfsCi deletion mutants showed no significant difference in colony diameter from the wild type on potato dextrose agar, but had significantly shorter germ tubes in the presence of 500 M capsidiol. Both mutants also produced smaller lesions on bell pepper fruits. Reintroduction of BcmfsCi restored germ tube elongation and lesion formation. In contrast, no significant reduction in lesion area was detected in the tomato fruit or tobacco leaf assays under the conditions tested. These results indicate that BcmfsCi contributes to germ tube elongation in the presence of capsidiol and to lesion formation on bell pepper fruits. This study suggests that infection by a broad-host-range pathogen may be supported not only by mechanisms that function across diverse hosts, but also by factors that respond to particular chemical environments.

papers.title: Distinct susceptibility of masked palm civet nasal epithelium to SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2
papers.abstract: Masked palm civets played an important role in the emergence of SARS-CoV-1, yet physiologically relevant civet respiratory epithelial models remain limited. Here, we establish air-liquid interface cultures from primary masked palm civet nasal epithelial cells. The cultures form a differentiated, barrier-forming epithelium containing ciliated, goblet, and club cell populations and recapitulate key features of native nasal tissue. Using parallel human and civet nasal cultures, we compare infection with SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2. In human cultures, both viruses show broadly similar replication kinetics. In civet cultures, SARS-CoV-1 replicates rapidly across donors and causes pronounced epithelial disruption, whereas SARS-CoV-2 replication is slower, less efficient, and more donor dependent. These findings reveal distinct compatibility of the two sarbecoviruses with differentiated civet nasal epithelium and establish a species-matched platform for investigating coronavirus host range and cross-species adaptation.
